The second definition of get_db_connection() (line 60) shadows the safe version defined at line 36 and calls itself unconditionally at line 61 (conn = get_db_connection()) with no base case, causing unbounded recursion (RecursionError / stack exhaustion). Because every route (index, create, edit, delete) and get_post() call get_db_connection(), any request that reaches a database call would crash the worker process - a denial of service. Note this block also contains indentation/syntax errors (lines 62-68) that currently prevent the module from importing at all.

In the version of get_db_connection() labeled 'Bad: Vulnerable to SQL Injection', post_id is concatenated directly into the SQL statement: conn.execute('SELECT * FROM posts WHERE id = '+post_id).fetchone(). The preceding validation (line 67, re.compile(r'^\d+$', re.M)) is a weak allowlist: with re.MULTILINE, '$' also matches before a newline, so an input such as '1\n<SQL>' passes the check and the raw value is concatenated into the query, enabling SQL injection. The correct parameterized form is shown in get_post() at lines 44-45 ('SELECT * FROM posts WHERE id = ?', (post_id,)).

The HTTP handler serves files based on the raw request path. The traversal filter (lines 10-11) uses re.match(r'/\.\.\/\.\.\/', self.path), which only rejects URLs that BEGIN with '/../../'. Any prefixed traversal such as /static/../../../../etc/passwd passes the check; line 14 then appends the raw path to os.getcwd() and line 22 opens the result and returns its contents (open(path).read()). This allows arbitrary local file read outside the web root, including sensitive system files. Resolve the path (os.path.realpath) and verify it stays within the intended document root.

extra.message: decrypt() base64-decodes a user-supplied session_id cookie and decrypts it with AES-CBC (line 19) then unpads the plaintext (line 20) with no MAC/HMAC integrity check. In do_GET (lines 25-29), any decryption or padding failure produces an HTTP 500 while valid padding produces a 200 response - a distinguishable padding oracle. An attacker submitting modified ciphertexts can exploit CBC padding-oracle techniques to recover cookie plaintext without knowing the key. Use an authenticated encryption mode (e.g., AES-GCM) or encrypt-then-MAC (HMAC).

The username recovered from the decrypted session_id cookie is interpolated into the HTML response via 'Hello %s' % username without any HTML encoding (the trailing comment 'needs encoding' acknowledges this). An attacker who controls the cookie plaintext (e.g., via the padding oracle or any cookie-injection vector) achieves reflected XSS in the victim's browser. HTML-encode user-derived values before writing them to the response.

context.check_hostname = False disables TLS hostname verification for the socket wrapped from ssl.create_default_context() (line 9). The HTTPS connection to website.com:443 will accept a certificate issued for any hostname, allowing a man-in-the-middle attacker to impersonate the server and read or inject traffic. Keep check_hostname True (the default); the inline comment confirms the check was deliberately disabled.

sign_for_payment() computes its signature as SHA256(secret + payment_information) - the secret-prefix MAC construction that is vulnerable to hash length-extension attacks. The signed payment parameters and signature are exposed in the redirect URL (lines 26-27); an attacker who observes one valid (message, signature) pair can forge valid signatures for an extended message (e.g., appended parameters such as an additional amount field) without knowing the secret, as the file's own comment notes ('payment information catted to secret & not using hmac'). Use hmac.new(secret, data, hashlib.sha256) instead.

extra.message: The /fetch endpoint takes the url query parameter and validates it only with url.startswith('https://insecurewebapp.com') before calling urllib.request.urlopen(url) (line 15) and returning the response body to the client. A startswith prefix check is a bypassable allowlist: https://insecurewebapp.com.attacker.tld/, https://insecurewebapp.com@169.254.169.254/ (userinfo trick), or https://insecurewebapp.com#@internal-host/ all pass the check while directing the request to an arbitrary host - a server-side request forgery that can reach internal hosts and cloud metadata endpoints, with the fetched content reflected to the requester. Parse the URL and validate the exact hostname (and scheme/port) against an allowlist.

urllib.request.urlopen(url) is called on a user-supplied URL without a timeout parameter. The default is no timeout, so a URL whose server accepts the connection but never responds blocks the Flask worker indefinitely; repeated requests exhaust the server's workers and deny service to legitimate users. This resource-exhaustion vector is distinct from the SSRF on the same line.
